intro.title: Before you press play
body: In 1921 Ireland was partitioned. Six north-eastern counties became Northern Ireland, part of the United Kingdom with its own parliament at Stormont. The rest became the Irish Free State, later the Republic of Ireland.

Northern Ireland's Protestant majority were mostly unionists who wanted to stay British. Its Catholic minority, about a third of the population, were mostly nationalists, many of whom wanted a united Ireland.

Fifty years of one-party unionist rule left Catholics facing discrimination in jobs, housing and voting. The Troubles began when a civil rights campaign collided with that system. Over 30 years, about 3,500 people were killed.
tips: Press play for a guided tour. The map flies to each event and back out.
Drag the timeline to scrub through time. Click any dot or tick to jump to it.
Watch the shaded areas: they show who controls the ground at that moment.

eras.title: Civil rights
eras.text: Catholics march for equal votes, homes and jobs. The marches meet police batons and loyalist counter-protests.

eras.title: Descent
eras.text: Riots, British troops on the streets, the IRA splits, and internment without trial.

eras.title: The worst years
eras.text: London rules directly. 1972 is the deadliest year of the conflict. Power-sharing is tried and collapses.

eras.title: Prison war
eras.text: Britain treats paramilitary prisoners as ordinary criminals. The prisons become the frontline, ending in the hunger strikes.

eras.title: Ballot box and Armalite
eras.text: Sinn Féin enters elections while the IRA campaign goes on. London and Dublin start working together over unionist heads.

eras.title: Peace process
eras.text: Ceasefires, a breakdown, and finally the Good Friday Agreement.
